In endgames this is huge: good bishop vs bad bishop is often a win all by itself, because the bad bishop is chained to defending pawns while your king walks in the front door.

examples.caption: White's bishop flies to h3 and attacks e6; Black's bishop — walled in by its own pawns on d5 and e6 — can only crawl to d7 to babysit them. One bishop hunts, the other guards. That's good vs bad.

drills.hint: Your pawns sit on dark squares — so which diagonal is wide open for your light-squared bishop?
drills.explain: Bg2! The fianchetto puts the bishop on the long light-squared diagonal, slicing toward d5 and b7. Your own pawns on dark squares will never block it — a textbook good bishop.

drills.hint: Your pawns on d4 and e5 block this bishop forever. Can you swap your worst piece for their best one?
drills.explain: Bb4! offers to trade the bad bishop (blocked by your own d4/e5 pawns) for Black's good dark-squared bishop. Trading your worst piece for their good one is a pure win — even though no material changes.

drills.hint: Your bishop owns the long dark diagonal — and White's king and rook are standing on the same line.
drills.explain: Bd4+! is a skewer: the check forces the king to step aside, and the bishop then slides all the way down the diagonal to capture the rook on a7. A good bishop on an open diagonal is a sniper.

lessons.title: Make a Plan: Ask Your Worst Piece
lessons.concept:
## Make a Plan: "What Does My Worst Piece Want?"

No tactics on the board? Don't shuffle and hope. Champions use a magic question between attacks:

> **"Which of my pieces is doing the LEAST — and where would it be happy?"**

**The routine (10 seconds):**
1. Look at each of your pieces, one by one.
2. Find the laziest one — the knight on the rim, the bishop staring at its own pawns, the rook behind a wall, the queen still on square one.
3. Find its dream square (an outpost, an open file, a juicy diagonal).
4. Make a move toward that square. That's your plan!

**Why it works:** a chess army wins when *every* piece has a job. One sleeping piece means you're playing down a piece — no blunder required. Improve your worst piece three times and your position often wins itself: suddenly tactics appear because all your pieces aim at the same target.

When you truly can't find a move, this question *always* gives you a good one.

examples.caption: Every white piece has a job except the sleepy c1-bishop. So the plan picks itself: Bg5! wakes it up and pins the f6-knight against the queen. Improve your worst piece and good things follow.

drills.hint: Which white piece is doing the least? (Hint: knights on the rim are dim.)
drills.explain: Nf4! The knight on the rim was White's worst piece. On f4 — protected by the g3-pawn — it jumps toward the center where it attacks in every direction. Worst piece improved, position improved.

drills.hint: Find Black's laziest piece, then find its dream square.
drills.explain: Re8! The a8-rook was asleep in the corner doing nothing. The open e-file is its dream home — now it controls the only open road and is ready to invade on e2 later.

drills.hint: One black piece hasn't moved all game and stares at its own pawn on e6. Where would it be happy?
drills.explain: Bb7! The buried c8-bishop was Black's worst piece — blocked by its own e6-pawn. On b7 it grabs the long open diagonal, aiming all the way at g2. Same bishop, totally new life.

title: Champion Habits
blurb: The off-the-board superpowers — blunder checks, clock skills, bounce-back routines, and tournament know-how — that turn a good player into a tough one.

lessons.title: The Blunder-Check Routine
lessons.concept:
## The Blunder-Check Routine

Most games under 1000 aren't won — they're *given away*. One hanging queen erases forty good moves. So champions run a safety routine before **every single move**, like a pilot's pre-flight checklist.

**Step 1 — Sit on your hands.** Literally. When you see a move you like, do NOT touch the piece. Put your hands under your legs or fold them. That tiny pause is where blunders go to die. The move you want to play instantly is often a trap; the move you play after ten seconds of checking is usually safe.

**Step 2 — The C-C-T scan.** Before your hand moves, answer three questions about the position *after* your planned move:

- **Checks:** Can my opponent check my king? Can I check theirs? Checks are forcing — always look at them first.
- **Captures:** What can they capture? Is anything of mine undefended or attacked more times than it's defended? What can I capture?
- **Threats:** What was their last move trying to do? What will they do next if I "pass"?

**Step 3 — Only then, move.** If the scan finds a problem, be happy — you just saved the game before it needed saving.

**For parents:** don't ask "did you win?" after games. Ask *"did you do your blunder check on every move?"* Praise the routine, not the result — the rating follows the routine. At home, you can practice by playing casual games where the only rule is: hands under legs, say "checks, captures, threats" out loud before moving. It feels slow for a week. Then it becomes automatic, and 100+ rating points show up almost by magic, because at this level the player who hangs fewer pieces simply wins.

lessons.title: Clock Craft
lessons.concept:
## Clock Craft

The clock is a piece. Learn to use it and you'll beat players who out-know you but can't manage time.

**The pacing rule of thumb:** in a 30-minute game, plan on about 40 moves — that's roughly 45 seconds a move on average. Easy recaptures and known opening moves should take 5 seconds; big decisions (trades, pawn breaks, anything scary) deserve 2–3 minutes. Glance at your clock every few moves the way a driver glances at mirrors — not staring, just aware.

**The two classic clock diseases:**
- **Speed-itis:** playing instantly because your opponent does. Their bad habit is not your boss. Use *your* clock — it's why you have one.
- **Freeze-itis:** burning 10 minutes on one move while your position is fine. If two moves both look okay after a real check, pick the safer one and go. A good move now beats a perfect move you never have time to find.

**Never flag a winning position.** Up a queen with 30 seconds left? Stop hunting for pretty checkmates. Make simple safe moves fast, trade pieces, push a pawn, promote, and mate with the basic technique you know cold. Many kids lose completely winning games because they sat back to admire the position. When low on time: safe moves, quick hands, no tours of the board.

**Practice at home:** play some 5-minute games just to get comfortable moving quickly, and some 15+ minute games where the rule is you *must* use at least 10 seconds per move. **For parents:** after a tournament game, one great question is "how much time did you have left?" Finishing a loss with 25 unspent minutes is a fixable habit, not a chess weakness.

lessons.title: Tilt Control: The Two-Loss Rule
lessons.concept:
## Tilt Control: The Two-Loss Rule

Every chess player on Earth loses. What separates champions is what happens in the ten minutes *after* a loss.

**What tilt looks like:** you lose a painful game, and in the next one you move too fast, skip your blunder check, and try to "win it back" with wild attacks. One loss becomes three. That spiral has a name — tilt — and it beats more kids than any opponent does.

**The Two-Loss Rule (for online play):** after two losses in a row, you are DONE for the session. Not "one more to fix it" — done. Close the app. The rating point you're trying to win back will still be there tomorrow; the tilted version of you will only donate more. Winners know when to stop.

**The between-rounds reset (for tournaments)** — after a loss, run this routine before the next round:
1. **Move your body.** Walk outside, get water, shake it off. Feelings live in the body; walking drains them.
2. **Say the lesson in one sentence.** "I stopped checking captures when I got winning." One sentence, then close the book — deep analysis waits until after the event.
3. **Reset sentence.** "New game, 0–0, my opponent has never seen my last game." Because it's true — the next game starts equal.

**For parents:** your face between rounds *is* the scoreboard. If a loss makes you visibly disappointed, your child learns to fear losing — and fear causes more losing. The magic words after a tough round: "Tell me later if you want. Want a snack?" Treat losses as boring and normal, and your child gets to treat them that way too.

lessons.title: Tournament Day
lessons.concept:
## Tournament Day

Tournaments are won in the boring details: sleep, food, and what you do *between* games.

**The night before:** pack the bag (scoresheets/notation book, two pens, water bottle, snacks, a jacket — playing halls run cold), and lights out at the normal time or earlier. One hour of lost sleep costs more rating points than any opening you could cram. No new chess the night before; you're not installing new software at midnight before launch.

**Morning of:** real breakfast with protein, not just sugar — a donut crashes exactly one hour into round one. Arrive 30+ minutes early so the pairings, the board, and the room all feel normal before the clock starts.

**Between rounds — the golden rules:**
- **Eat small, drink water.** Little snacks (fruit, nuts, sandwich) beat one giant lunch that makes round three sleepy. Most "second-half collapses" are really hunger and dehydration.
- **Rest your brain.** A walk outside beats an hour of blitz in the hallway. Chess between rounds spends the exact fuel you need for the next game.
- **Do NOT deep-review games mid-event** — especially losses. A one-sentence lesson, then done. Replaying a heartbreaker between rounds guarantees you carry it into the next round.

**After the event (this is where improvement actually lives):** within a day or two, go through every game — *especially* the losses — with a coach, a parent, or an engine. Find the one moment each game turned. Write down one thing to work on. That review habit is the difference between playing tournaments and *learning* from them.

**For parents:** your jobs are logistics, snacks, and calm. Results are the player's department; the schedule is yours. A kid who is fed, rested, and relaxed plays 100 points stronger than the same kid tired and pressured.

lessons.title: Notation & Touch-Move
lessons.concept:
## Notation & Touch-Move: OTB Rules That Win Points

Over-the-board chess has rules that don't exist online — and knowing them cold wins real points every tournament.

**Touch-move:** if you touch a piece (yours or your opponent's) on purpose, you must move it or capture it if there's a legal way. Let go of a piece on a square, and the move is final — "oops" doesn't undo it. So build the habit: **decide with your eyes, not your fingers.** Hands stay in your lap until the choice is 100% made. If you need to straighten a crooked piece, first say **"adjust"** (or "j'adoube"), *then* touch it — and only do this on your own turn.

**Notation:** in most rated events you must write every move (yours and your opponent's). Do it even when it's optional, because your scoresheet is a superpower:
- It's your **evidence** for claims like threefold repetition or the fifty-move rule, and it settles any dispute about what happened.
- It slows you down half a beat each move — a free, built-in blunder check.
- It's the only way to review the game afterward and actually improve.

Write the move *after* you play it, keep it legible, and if you fall behind in time trouble, catch up when the storm passes (rules typically let you stop notating under five minutes).

**Know how to get help:** if something weird happens — illegal move, clock problem, opponent's phone buzzing — **stop the clock and raise your hand** for the tournament director. That is always allowed, never rude, and it's *your* job, not your parent's; parents can't approach the board during play. Practicing these mechanics at home — real board, real clock, writing moves in casual games — makes tournament day feel like just another Tuesday.
